meta.title: Who really said "Attitude is a little thing that makes a big difference"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Churchill. Quote Investigator traces the saying to Zig Ziglar's See You at the Top (1977), p. 204 — where the wording is subtly different.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Attitude is a little thing that makes a big difference'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Churchill and not Roosevelt. The earliest known use is Zig Ziglar's, in See You at the Top (1977), p. 204 — worded slightly differently.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1926–2012 · American motivational speaker and sales author
answer.sourceLine: Widely and reasonably credited to Ziglar: Quote Investigator ↗ reports that the earliest known use of the saying is his, on page 204 of the 1977 Pelican edition of See You at the Top, verified on paper. Two things keep this short of settled: his sentence there reads “Attitude is the ‘little’ thing that makes the big difference,” not the poster wording, and QI adds that it is not clear whether Ziglar coined the expression. The Winston Churchill and Theodore Roosevelt credits that dominate the internet have no substantive support at all.

source.excerpt: Attitude is the “little” thing that makes the big difference. The story of life proves that it is often the minute things that spell the differences between triumph and tragedy, success and failure, victory or defeat.
trail: 1895 and 1920 — the “little thing / big difference” contrast is already stock phrasing, used of amateur photography in Recreation magazine and of advertising layout in Roy S. Durstine’s Making Advertisements and Making Them Pay, per Quote Investigator ↗.

1977 — Zig Ziglar applies the frame to attitude on page 204 of See You at the Top (Pelican Publishing, Gretna, Louisiana), the earliest use QI ↗ has located — QI cites the twenty-seventh printing of January 1982. A separate 1977 Pelican abridged educational edition of the book is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗; it is not the printing QI verified, and its pagination does not match.
1996 — John Mason’s Conquering An Enemy Called Average (Insight International, Tulsa) prints the modern wording at page 48, unattributed, according to QI’s scan-verified citation ↗.
2002–2003 — the famous names arrive: a Roosevelt variant in A Call to America, then a flat Churchill credit in Michael Massey’s Knowledge, page 53. QI ↗ finds substantive support for neither.

source.rightsHolder: The estate of Zig Ziglar and Pelican Publishing Company
source.rightsNote: See You at the Top is a 1970s Pelican Publishing title — the edition whose page 204 was verified is dated 1977, and catalogue records place the book’s first appearance in the mid-1970s. Either way it was published decades after the 1931 United States public-domain threshold, so the passage remains in copyright to Zig Ziglar’s estate and his publisher. The short quotation is reproduced here for identification and comment.

author.heading: Who Zig Ziglar was
author.metaLine: 1926–2012 · American motivational speaker, salesman and author
author.bio: Hilary Hinton “Zig” Ziglar was born in Coffee County, Alabama in 1926 and died in Plano, Texas in 2012. He worked as a salesman before becoming one of the defining voices of American motivational speaking, and wrote more than thirty books through Ziglar, Inc., the company he founded in 1977. See You at the Top — the Pelican Publishing title in which this saying first appears — is the book that made his name.

misattribution.heading: Two wrong names, and one right name with the wrong words
misattribution.intro: Almost every viral version of this line carries the wrong name — and the version that carries the right name carries the wrong words.

items.why: This is the ascription Quote Investigator ↗ set out to test, and it fails. QI reports the expression is not listed in Churchill by Himself, Richard Langworth’s definitive collection of Churchill quotations, and that it has located no substantive evidence linking the statement to him. The earliest Churchill credit QI documents is from 2003 — Michael Massey’s Knowledge, where the line runs as a chapter epigraph on page 53. It also appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s Churchill page ↗, in any section.

The expanded form — “Your attitude about who you are and what you have is a very little thing that makes a very big difference” — was credited to Roosevelt in the 2002 anthology A Call to America, edited by Bryan Curtis. QI ↗ finds no substantive support for that credit either, and records the line only as another similar saying about attitude that was being disseminated by 2002.

Ziglar is very probably the source of the thought, but the sentence on the poster is not his sentence. On page 204 of the 1977 Pelican edition of See You at the Top, which QI ↗ verified on paper, he wrote “Attitude is the ‘little’ thing that makes the big difference” — definite articles, scare quotes around little. The smoothed indefinite-article form that circulates today is first documented in John Mason’s 1996 Conquering An Enemy Called Average, page 48, where it closes a short passage with no credit to Ziglar at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea and the earliest known wording are Zig Ziglar’s, from See You at the Top — but Quote Investigator ↗ keeps the honest caveat attached: it is not clear whether he coined the expression, since writers had been contrasting a “little thing” with a “big difference” since at least 1895, more than eighty years before him.

context.heading: Why a sales book ended up sounding like a war leader
lead: The saying travels on office posters, and posters want a name with weight — which is how a piece of 1970s American sales motivation ended up in the mouth of a British wartime prime minister. The question that prompted Quote Investigator’s inquiry ↗ came from someone looking at exactly such a poster, and noting drily that “a distinguished attribution is a little thing that can make a big difference in the perception of a quotation.”

The rhetorical move underneath the line is far older than any of the names attached to it. QI records writers setting a “little thing” against a “big difference” in an 1895 letter to Recreation magazine about amateur photography, and again in a 1920 book on advertising by Roy S. Durstine — decades before anyone pointed the frame at attitude.
detailsBody: 1895 and 1920 — the “little thing / big difference” contrast is already a stock phrase, used of photography and of advertising layout, with no connection to attitude.
1977 — Ziglar applies it to attitude in See You at the Top, page 204: “Attitude is the ‘little’ thing that makes the big difference.” This is the earliest use Quote Investigator has located.
1996 — John Mason’s Conquering An Enemy Called Average prints the smoothed modern wording, unattributed, at the end of a short motivational passage.

2002 and 2003 — the line acquires famous names: a Theodore Roosevelt variant in the anthology A Call to America, then a straight Winston Churchill credit as a chapter epigraph in Michael Massey’s Knowledge.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes it has located no substantive support for assigning the saying to Winston Churchill or Theodore Roosevelt, and that the earliest usage belongs to Zig Ziglar though it is not clear whether he coined the expression.

Quote Investigator cites Zig Ziglar, See You at the Top, 1977, Pelican Publishing Company, Gretna, Louisiana, Segment Five: Attitude, Chapter One, page 204 (verified on paper), reading: 'Attitude is the "little" thing that makes the big difference. The story of life proves that it is often the minute things that spell the differences between triumph and tragedy, success and failure, victory or defeat.'
Quote Investigator states the expression is not listed in 'Churchill by Himself', a comprehensive collection of Churchill quotations edited by Richard Langworth.

Quote Investigator documents the exact popular wording 'Attitude is a little thing that makes a big difference' in John Mason, Conquering An Enemy Called Average, 1996, Nugget Number 17, page 48, Insight International, Tulsa, Oklahoma (verified with scans), unattributed.

Quote Investigator documents a Theodore Roosevelt credit for the variant 'Your attitude about who you are and what you have is a very little thing that makes a very big difference' in 'A Call to America', edited by Bryan Curtis, 2002, Rutledge Hill Press.

Quote Investigator documents the Churchill credit by 2003 in Michael Massey, 'Knowledge: How to Be an Effective and Emotionally Intelligent Leader', epigraph to Chapter 8, page 53, Troubador Publishing.

Quote Investigator cites earlier 'little things make a big difference' phrasing in Recreation magazine, May 1895, page 390 (about photography) and in Roy S. Durstine, Making Advertisements and Making Them Pay, 1920, page 164 (about advertisements).

Zig Ziglar was born 6 November 1926 in Coffee County, Alabama and died 28 November 2012 in Plano, Texas; he was an American author, salesman and motivational speaker who founded Ziglar, Inc. in 1977 and wrote over 30 books.
The Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for Zig Ziglar's 'See you at the top', published by Pelican Pub. Co., Gretna, La., dated 1977.
Open Library work OL1923964W is 'See You at the Top' by Zig Ziglar, with Pelican Publishing Company among its listed publishers.

Wikiquote's Zig Ziglar page does not include the line 'Attitude is a little thing that makes a big difference' or the variant 'the little thing that makes the big difference' among its sourced quotations.
Wikiquote's Winston Churchill page does not contain 'Attitude is a little thing that makes a big difference' in any section, including its Disputed and Misattributed sections.
